claims.claim: Intel's structural thesis couples x86/AI compute demand to domestic leading-edge logic manufacturing and advanced packaging; 18A/18A-P and 14A are intended to turn process capability into both internal product advantage and external foundry capacity.

causalEdges.to: Intel Products and advanced-node wafer demand
causalEdges.mechanism: higher-performance workloads pull premium CPUs and leading-edge process capacity
causalEdges.falsifier: product share or premium mix reverses despite market growth

causalEdges.mechanism: domestic leading-edge logic capacity can serve internal products and external customers
causalEdges.falsifier: yields fail to mature or committed external demand remains insufficient for economic utilization

risks.risk: TSMC and other foundries remain substitutes for external customers; internal-product demand currently dominates Intel Foundry utilization.

unknowns.unknown: Committed external 14A demand sufficient to support economic fab utilization is not yet established.

claims.claim: Turnaround evidence is real but not complete: Q2 Foundry revenue rose while the segment still lost $2.089B, and substantially all foundry activity still supports Intel Products internally.

risks.risk: Foundry Q2 operating loss was $2.089B on $5.765B segment revenue; economics remain deeply negative despite improvement.
Only $293M of Q2 Foundry revenue was external and much of that reflected Altera's deconsolidation, limiting evidence of independent external foundry traction.
18A early-ramp wafers carry higher costs, and 14A expansion pace depends on committed demand.

contradictions.contradiction: Leading-edge process milestones and revenue growth coexist with large foundry losses and limited true external revenue.

unknowns.unknown: Normalized external foundry margins and durable utilization remain unproven.
